video_metadata.working_title: KENTUCKY 1968 Cold Case Identified After 30 Years — The Tent Girl Was Barbara Taylor
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: A young woman found wrapped in green canvas beside U.S. 25 near Georgetown, Kentucky, on May 17, 1968, stayed nameless for 30 years until the finder's son-in-law, Todd Matthews, matched her to a sister's online post, and mitochondrial DNA confirmed she was Barbara Ann 'Bobbie' Hackmann Taylor; her killing has never been solved and no one was ever charged.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turned into stubborn hope: a nameless woman given back her name by an ordinary man with a computer

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: Barbara Ann 'Bobbie' Hackmann Taylor (the victim, known for 30 years only as 'Tent Girl'); story hero: J. Todd Matthews
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: 24 when she disappeared in late 1967 (born September 12, 1943). In 1968 investigators estimated her age at 16 to 19.
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Young wife and mother of an infant daughter, recently moved from Illinois to Lexington, Kentucky, with her husband George Earl Taylor, a carnival worker.
protagonist.location: Lexington, Kentucky (last known residence, late 1967); body found beside U.S. Route 25 near its intersection with Interstate 75, north of Georgetown, Scott County, Kentucky.
protagonist.physical_description: 1968 description: about 5 feet 1 inch, about 110 to 115 pounds, reddish-brown hair, estimated 16 to 19 years old. Re-examination in 1998 by forensic anthropologist Dr. Emily Craig estimated 20 to 30.
protagonist.background_brief: Born in Illinois on September 12, 1943; grew up in the East St. Louis / Collinsville area of Illinois in a large family with six siblings (secondary source). In 1967 she moved to Kentucky with her husband without telling her family in Illinois. She had an eight-month-old daughter when she vanished.
protagonist.psychological_profile: No documented personal statements survive in the sources found. Her sister Rosemary kept searching for her for three decades.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: Her family called her Bobbie. Her sister Rosemary Westbrook was still posting online appeals for her in 1997-1998.
protagonist.nickname_or_alias_if_any: Bobbie; 'Tent Girl' (name given by press and public because of the tent-like canvas she was wrapped in)

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Wilbur Riddle
characters.key_actions_they_took: While collecting old glass insulators along U.S. 25 north of Georgetown, found a bundle of heavy green canvas containing the body of a young woman and alerted authorities. Described in accounts as a well driller by trade (secondary).

characters.name: J. Todd Matthews
characters.role_in_story: Riddle's son-in-law; amateur investigator who identified her
characters.key_actions_they_took: Heard the story on Halloween night 1987 at 17 from Lori Riddle; married Lori (1988 per one source); researched for about a decade, at first in person; built a Tent Girl website in 1997; in January 1998 (some accounts say February) found Rosemary Westbrook's post and emailed her; later co-founded the Doe Network and worked at NamUs
characters.notable_quotes: 'It took 30 years, and ultimately, I was called to the Department of Justice to develop the NamUs program in 2007.' (NBC)

characters.name: Lori Riddle Matthews
characters.key_actions_they_took: Told Todd and friends the story of the body her father found, on Halloween night 1987

characters.name: George Earl Taylor
characters.role_in_story: Barbara's husband; carnival worker; described by sources as the prime suspect
characters.key_actions_they_took: Did not report her missing; told her family she had left him for another man
characters.notable_quotes: None verified. Died of cancer in October 1987. Never charged, never tried, never convicted.

characters.name: Dr. Emily Craig
characters.key_actions_they_took: Examined the exhumed remains in Frankfort in March 1998; estimated age at death 20 to 30

characters.name: Kenneth Grant
characters.key_actions_they_took: Preliminary examination at St. Joseph Hospital (single secondary source)

characters.name: Dr. Frank Cleveland

characters.name: Scott County Sheriff's Office
characters.key_actions_they_took: Announced on April 23, 1998, that the Tent Girl was Barbara Ann Hackmann Taylor

Barbara disappears; she has an eight-month-old daughter. Her husband files no missing-person report and tells her family she left him for another man

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.exact_location: Roadside of U.S. Route 25 near Interstate 75, north of Georgetown, Kentucky
the_moment.what_is_happening: Wilbur Riddle, looking for old glass telephone-line insulators, finds a heavy bundle of green canvas; inside is the body of a young woman
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: No one reports her missing; no one claims her; she is buried as TENT GIRL for 30 years
the_moment.ironic_twist: The man who finally named her was the finder's own son-in-law, who first heard the story as a Halloween tale at 17

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Who was the girl in the tent, and why did no one come looking for her for 30 years?

the_method._instructions: How was the case finally resolved? Technical details for a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Amateur internet comparison of missing and unidentified listings, confirmed by exhumation and mitochondrial DNA comparison with a sister
step_by_step_explanation: Matthews gathered the known description of the Tent Girl (age estimate, height, weight, hair, date and place found).
In 1997 he built a website about her and searched early online missing-person listings.
In January 1998 he found a post by Rosemary Westbrook describing her sister who vanished from Lexington in late 1967.
He emailed Westbrook; her description matched the details on the headstone.
Authorities exhumed the remains on March 2, 1998; Dr. Emily Craig re-examined them.
Bone and teeth were compared with a cheek or saliva sample from Westbrook; the DNA matched.
On April 23, 1998, the Scott County Sheriff's Office announced the identification.
the_method.why_it_worked: For the first time, the description of an unknown body and the description of a missing woman were both public and searchable in the same place; one person read both.

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: Small rings of DNA in the energy-making parts of cells, passed almost unchanged from a mother to all her children, so sisters share the same sequence; it survives well in old bone and teeth because each cell holds many copies.
Lifting a buried body from the grave with legal permission for examination.
A scientist who reads age, sex and history from bones.

the_method.scale_of_operation: One man, one computer, one email, one sister; roughly ten years of private effort

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: The 1960s-1990s missing and unidentified persons system as a whole
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Missing-person reports and descriptions of unknown dead were supposed to be compared so families could find their loved ones
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: No missing-person report was filed for Barbara; there was no national, public, searchable database matching unidentified remains to missing adults; the age estimate (16-19) was well below her real age (24); the estimated time of death was shorter than the months she had actually been missing
specific_incompetence_examples: No missing-person report was ever filed by her husband
Identification came from a volunteer, not from an official system
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: Barbara disappeared from Lexington, about a dozen miles from where she was found, yet stayed nameless for 30 years.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Scott County authorities (coroner and sheriff); Kentucky forensic anthropologist in 1998
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Estimated age 16-19; estimated recent time of death
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: Rosemary Westbrook's online listing found by Todd Matthews in January 1998
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: Victim identified after 30 years; killer never identified in court

the_confrontation.scene_description: Announcement that the Tent Girl had a name; funeral in Georgetown two days later
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: The original TENT GIRL headstone was kept, with a new marker bearing her real name added beneath it

legal_resolution.current_status: Unsolved homicide. George Earl Taylor, described by sources as the prime suspect, died of cancer in October 1987 and was never charged, tried or convicted; he is presumed innocent. No later charges reported as of October 2026.
